articles.title: NATO fighter jet cleared to shoot down Russian missile over Poland as Warsaw pushes for US troops
articles.summary: Poland renewed its push for permanent U.S. troops after a Russian drone entered its airspace Nov. 24, days after three Kh-101 missile violations.
articles.body: Poland announced Tuesday it had renewed its push for a permanent U.S. military presence in the country after two Russian airspace incursions in four days, including one in which a Swedish fighter jet under NATO command was cleared to shoot down a Russian cruise missile but held its fire. The latest incursion came overnight Nov. 24, when a Russian drone briefly entered Polish airspace during attacks on Ukraine, four days after three Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles had crossed into Poland, prompting NATO to scramble fighter jets and bolster air defenses along its eastern flank. Poland's chargé d'affaires in Washington, Bogdan Klich, said Tuesday that he briefed the White House National Security Council on the violations and renewed Warsaw's call to permanently station American troops in the NATO member country. US URGES AMERICANS IN HISTORIC REGION TO STAY ALERT AFTER 'DANGEROUS' AIRSPACE INCIDENT "Yesterday, I briefed the U.S. National Security Council on the violation of Polish airspace by Russian Kh-101 missiles and once again discussed the issue of the permanent deployment of U.S. troops in Poland," Klich wrote on X. The new diplomatic push follows the incidents involving Russian assets and heightened concerns that Moscow's war in Ukraine will spill into NATO territory. The Nov. 20 incursion involved a Swedish JAS 39 Gripen pilot operating under NATO command who was authorized to engage a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile, according to Lt. Gen. Ireneusz Nowak, commander of Poland’s Armed Forces Operational Command, as reported by The Kyiv Independent. NATO's Combined Air Operations Centre in Uedem, Germany, issued conditional authorization to fire, but the pilot could not positively identify the object visually or through the aircraft's onboard electro-optical systems because of severe weather, Nowak said. No weapons were fired. SUPERSONIC RUSSIAN JETS TRIGGER JOINT SCRAMBLE BY NATO ALLIES AMID PUTIN 'CLOWNS' JAB Polish authorities monitored 11 potentially threatening aerial objects during the attack, three of which entered the country's airspace, according to Nowak. The Swedish Armed Forces said its jets had tracked several unidentified objects over Poland during the mission, which lasted several hours under difficult weather conditions. Polish F-16 fighter jets, a Swedish Saab 340 early warning aircraft, a Dutch aerial refueling aircraft and ground-based air defense systems were also supporting the operation. Polish prosecutors confirmed Sunday that debris recovered at three locations belonged to Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles, revising an initial military assessment that one of the objects might have been a drone, according to reports. RUSSIA PREPARING HYBRID ATTACKS ON NATO'S EASTERN FLANK, INTELLIGENCE WARNS Preliminary findings indicated the missiles were manufactured in October or November 2026 at a factory in Dubna in Russia's Moscow region, prosecutors said. The second incursion happened overnight Nov. 24, when a Russian drone entered Polish airspace from Ukraine during another wave of Russian strikes on Ukraine. Polish forces tracked the unmanned aircraft and received authorization to shoot it down but did not fire after it changed course and headed east, citing potential risks to civilians and property on the ground. Deputy Defense Minister Paweł Zalewski said Polish authorities believed the violation was deliberate. "It's hard to imagine this being a coincidence, so we assume it was an intentional act," Zalewski told RMF FM, according to Reuters. After an emergency meeting of the North Atlantic Council on Monday, Nov. 23, NATO's supreme allied commander in Europe went on to authorize the forward deployment of an Airborne Warning and Control System, or AWACS, aircraft to Poland. NATO WARNS PUTIN COULD STRIKE BEFORE EUROPEAN ARMY RESPONDS, POINTS TO US AS MILITARY MODEL "All Allies stand in full solidarity with Poland. NATO remains united, ready, and committed to defending against any threat," NATO spokesperson Allison Hart said on X and as Warsaw summoned Russia's ambassador, according to Reuters. In September, Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski said U.S. and Polish officials were working toward an agreement that could accommodate up to 10,000 American troops. Roughly 7,000 U.S. troops were stationed in Poland on a rotational basis at the time while a permanent installation would expand Washington's military commitment along NATO's eastern flank. "We want the kind of U.S. presence that would reassure us but not be threatening to Russia," Sikorski said during a Council on Foreign Relations event in New York, Bloomberg reported. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP President Donald Trump has previously voiced his support for a permanent U.S. military base in Poland, although Washington has also reviewed American troop deployments across Europe.

articles.title: Hostage situation reported in Colombia as armed men flee into supermarket
articles.summary: President Abelardo de la Espriella says police and military have been deployed as situation unfolds in Cartagena.
articles.body:
About 25 people are being held hostage at a supermarket in the Colombian city of Cartagena, where a group of armed men fled after an unsuccessful attempt to rob an armoured vehicle.

President Abelardo de la Espriella said on Tuesday that police and armed forces have been deployed to the scene.

He explained that the robbers sought refuge in a nearby store after security camera operators alerted police to the attempted robbery.

“Thirty people were kidnapped, five of whom have already been released. They are older women,” said de la Espriella. “All the capabilities of our various security forces have now been deployed, including special units.”

Images from the Reuters news agency showed heavily armed police and military personnel outside the Exito supermarket in the neighbourhood of La Castellana.

Unverified footage shared on social media appeared to show people inside the market kneeling against the windows with their hands bound.

The incident comes as de la Espriella, who campaigned on a promise to crack down on crime, faces a series of high-profile incidents that underscore the country’s ongoing issues with violence and insecurity.

The president made his remarks from the city of Villavicencio, where he had travelled in the aftermath of a recent car bombing the government has attributed to an armed group.

Already, politicians like former left-wing President Gustavo Petro have weighed in on the incident, blaming failures in de la Espriella’s security platform.

“The root cause of this violence is the impoverishment of the population, brought about by the collapse of the tourism sector,” Petro, de la Espriella’s predecessor, wrote on social media.

“Destroying tourism — through state-sanctioned violence, such as the desecration of corpses, and by making death the central theme of presidential discourse — has dismantled a dynamic source of wealth that once attracted 7 million foreign tourists.”

De la Espriella beat Petro’s handpicked successor, Senator Ivan Cepeda, in a June 21 run-off election.

articles.title: Four former detainees allege they were raped, subject to forced labor at a Louisiana ICE facility
articles.summary: Four formerly detained immigrants said they were subjected to rape, sexual assault, anti-LGBTQ harassment and a forced labor scheme at an ICE detention center in Louisiana.
articles.body: Four formerly detained immigrants said they were subjected to rape, sexual assault, anti-LGBTQ harassment and a forced labor scheme at an ICE detention center in Louisiana. The four filed a federal lawsuit Monday against GEO Group, the private prison company behind the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center in Basile, Louisiana, as well as former assistant warden Emmanuel Reyes and former detention officer David Courvelle. The detention center is the largest in the nation for female immigrant detainees. They “endured a months-long nightmare of rape, sexual abuse, degrading harassment, and hard manual labor that targeted primarily transgender and non-binary detained people,” according to the lawsuit. Luis Renteria-Gonzalez, Mario Garcia-Valenzuela, Kenia Campos-Flores and Jane Doe said in the lawsuit that between 2023 and 2025 they were repeatedly abused by Reyes and Courvelle and forced to perform sex acts and hard manual labor under threats to themselves and their families. Renteria-Gonzalez and Garcia-Valenzuela are transgender men and Campos-Flores is nonbinary. “They suffered horrific, abusive conditions at the hands of employees of the GEO Group,” Susan Meyers, the senior supervising attorney with the Southern Poverty Law Center, told NBC News. GEO Group did not immediately respond to a request for comment. NBC News was unable to reach Reyes and Courvelle. Courvelle was sentenced to three years in federal prison in June after pleading guilty to sexual abuse of a different detainee. “Reyes coerced plaintiffs to perform hard physical labor, sex acts, or both, threatening them with death, deportation, further sexual abuse, physical harm, and harm to their families and loved ones,” according to a statement announcing the lawsuit. The physical labor and custodial work involved stripping floors, sanitizing housing units and facility spaces and moving heavy supplies and machinery without protective equipment, the lawsuit said, adding that the plaintiffs suffered physical injuries and exposure to toxic fumes. Reyes is accused in the lawsuit of telling Renteria-Gonzalez, “If you think you are a man, I’m going to treat you like a man.” Reyes abused his power to sexually assault the detainees in areas hidden from surveillance cameras, stalk them, view their naked bodies on surveillance camera footage and harass people in the middle of the night, according to the lawsuit. The lawsuit also alleges that after Doe turned down an offer to join Reyes’ “cleaning crew,” he stalked and harassed her, groped her and forced Doe to perform sex acts on him under threats to her life if she refused. Reyes left the facility voluntarily in 2024, Meyers said. It was unclear if he was employed at another facility. GEO Group did not immediately respond to a request for comment about Reyes’ employment status. The lawsuit also accused Courvelle of sexually assaulting Garcia-Valenzuela multiple times and forcing Renteria-Gonzalez and Garcia-Valenzuela to stand guard outside a closet while he raped a woman who was also detained there. “The treatment and the conditions that they had us living in, nobody should go through that,” Renteria-Gonzalez said in the statement. “It’s unbelievable that this happened under the care of the people who are supposed to protect us.” Sarah Decker, a senior staff attorney at the Robert and Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center, said the four former detainees did not suffer in silence. “They screamed for help. They filed a complaint with every avenue that was available to them,” she said. Meyers said that despite them coming forward with the allegations, “in many cases things got worse, because what they found was that it opened them up to retaliatory actions” such as solitary confinement. Garcia-Valenzuela said in a statement, “We were looked down upon like the sole of someone’s shoe.” “What we experienced there was a true nightmare,” Garcia-Valenzuela said. “For the rest of my life, I will live with the aftereffects of the torture and abuse I endured.” There have been previous accusations of sexual abuse at the facility, including in 2022, when a Prison Rape Elimination Act audit by the Department of Homeland Security documented four sexual abuse allegations that included one staff-on-detainee allegation and three detainee-on-detainee allegations. Two of the sexual abuse allegations were substantiated, including one against a staff member who resigned the day the allegation was made, according to the audit report. All four cases were investigated and closed. The report does not say how GEO Group responded to the four cases. The auditor found in the report that the detention center met 36 standards, exceeded one standard, and was out of compliance with two standards: accommodating detainees with disabilities and detainees who are limited English proficient, and detainee education. The facility entered into a 180-day corrective plan for those two standards and was later found to be in compliance.

articles.title: 6 years after split, Akalis & BJP tie up for Punjab assembly polls
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: After six years of separation marked by AAP's rise in Punjab, BJP and Shiromani Akali Dal on Tuesday renewed their alliance ahead of assembly
articles.body: NEW DELHI: After six years of separation marked by AAP's rise in Punjab, BJP and Shiromani Akali Dal on Tuesday renewed their alliance ahead of assembly polls, with home minister Amit Shah recognising the regional party as the "big brother" in the tie-up and claimant to the chief minister's chair in case NDA returns to office after a decade.Shah was joined by SAD president Sukhbir Singh Badal and BJP chief Nitin Nabin at the announcement, timed to coincide with Guru Nanak's birth anniversary, exuding confidence in their victory and the governing AAP's wipeout in the polls to be held early next year.The Akalis had broken away from NDA over the now-scrapped farm laws.The revival of the alliance after a period which saw SAD's fortunes nosedive and BJP achieve limited success in expanding its base outside its influence in urban areas brings NDA right back into the reckoning in a state where AAP and Congress were being seen as the main election contenders.BJP and SAD are banking on the revival of the social compact between the former's base among Hindus and the latter's once-formidable farmer constituency. Much will depend on whether their renewed chemistry will enthuse their traditional voters in a crowded battlefield.Amit Shah: BJP-SAD pact not merely political, it’s an emotional bondPM Modi, whose meeting with Badal in Parliament complex on Aug 7 was the first clear indication of the tie-up, was emphatic in his endorsement of what he called a "natural alliance"."Putting Punjab and the welfare of Punjabis first. I am extremely delighted that Shiromani Akali Dal returns to NDA family and that too on the Parkash Purab of Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji. Ours is a natural alliance that will ensure Punjab gets pro-people governance that takes the state to new heights of progress," home minister Amit Shah said. Modi will be in Moga on Dec 8 to attend a rally to mark Parkash Singh Badal's birth anniversary. Shah said, "The alliance between BJP and SAD is not merely political; it is an emotional bond rooted in mutual trust and Punjab's history. NDA is now complete with Akali Dal's return.""A tidal wave has started today," SAD's Sukhbir Singh Badal said, claiming the alliance would bag 100 seats in the 117-member assembly.Shah was quick to emphasise the alliance's emotive symbolism of Hindu-Sikh brotherhood in the border state with a history of social tensions and spells of militancy; Nabin too described it as a "natural alliance", and Badal invoked his father's description of their ties as "nau-maas da rishta" (together like nail and flesh). Jana Sangh, BJP's political predecessor, had allied with Akalis too. Shah's announcement that SAD will be the senior partner - Badal being the obvious CM face even though no such announcement was made - despite its shrinking base, underscores BJP's recognition that its Sikh ally should lead the alliance and look like a credible contender for office. The BJP, however, is expected to contest a bigger number of seats than the 23 it used to in the alliance.Akali's 10-year stint in office, with BJP as junior partner, ended in 2017 with their massive defeat at the hands of Congress as a big chunk of its core voters revolted over the government's alleged mishandling of sacrilege incidents and issues of drug abuse and corruption, creating a fertile ground for AAP's rise and its subsequent sweep in 2022.Congress general secretary in-charge of Punjab Sachin Pilot said, "It's a compromised alliance, a desperate alliance. BJP and SAD have not revealed why they parted ways six years ago, what were the reasons that SAD and BJP left each other. Have the GoI and BJP given any assurance to the country on MSP, have they apologised for the three black farm laws, and what is the SAD view on the hundreds of protesters who died on the Delhi border in the farmers' protest? Both parties had no political space left in the state, and they have chosen to join hands."Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Nuclear test veterans will get full truth, says Burnham, as he confirms independent panel
articles.summary: The prime minister says a Hillsborough-style independent panel will examine the health legacy of Britain's Cold War-era atomic programme.
articles.body:
Andy Burnham has told nuclear test veterans they will get "the full truth" as he confirmed plans for an investigation into the health legacy of Britain's Cold War-era atomic programme.

The prime minister has ordered an independent panel modelled on the Hillsborough disaster investigation to assess the potential impact of testing exercises in the 1950s and 1960s.

Burnham told veterans and their families that the government would treat the process with the "utmost seriousness" as he vowed to set up a "gold standard" investigation.

The Ministry of Defence (MoD) has for decades denied it covered up the impact of radiation on troops ordered to carry out nuclear weapons tests.

A BBC Newsnight special programme heard reaction from veterans, including John Morris, a laundry operator at a nuclear test site who went on to develop cancer and lost a four-month-old son. He believes both were linked to radiation exposure.

He said: "Seventy-two years ago I was an 18-year-old, sent to Christmas Island, totally unaware of what I was being led into.

"I am here today and I am looking for, and sincerely hope we will get, justice."

Veterans who were involved in the tests, predominantly carried out in Australia and the South Pacific, have long called for a full investigation into the long-term health effects it had on them and their children.

Many of the surviving veterans say they were more likely to develop a range of illnesses in the years that followed, while their descendants say they have suffered an increased risk of hereditary illnesses and fertility problems.

Veterans have recounted being ordered to fly through radioactive clouds without protection, witnessing atomic explosions with nothing to shield them from the fallout, and living on sand they believe was contaminated with nuclear material.

The announcement of an independent panel is the culmination of years of campaigning by the LABRATS group and others, and comes 14 years after a legal challenge at the UK Supreme Court failed.

Many veterans have died in the decades since the tests, but some of those still alive shared their stories with Newsnight on Tuesday.

Brian Unthank says he witnessed three hydrogen bomb explosions in the Pacific without protective equipment and went to on develop multiple skin cancers.

He said: "I've always wanted to get a prime minister... to stand up in Parliament and make a total, abject apology for the total mess-up of the way they treated us veterans and the families through this 74 years.

"Next year is our 75th year of misery. Let's get it done today."

Barbara Quick, whose father served in the RAF Police on Christmas Island - a major site for UK and US nuclear testing in the Pacific Ocean - told BBC Newsnight she had never been able to have children and two of her sister's children had died. She blames health complications arising from their father's exposure to radiation.

She said: "If you were higher personnel you got the gas mask, you got the suit - but my father was told to turn his collar up, turn his back and cover his eyes."

Steve Purse, whose father was a nuclear test veteran, was born with complex disabilities he says have never been fully diagnosed. He told BBC Newsnight the announcement was "huge" but that the panel must be allowed to provide full disclosure.

He said: "No-one has listened to us like this before, it's a moment of history."

Before becoming prime minister earlier this year, Burnham told BBC Newsnight the nuclear veterans had been subjected to a "criminal cover-up on an industrial scale" and backed calls for an investigation.

On Tuesday, he told campaigners at Downing Street: "All I can say is you know the courage you've shown, the dignity you've shown through the whole thing, given everything that happened, is honestly something that we just are in awe of.

"Your patience, your strength, your determination - and we will make sure that this process moves as quickly as possible to get you what you long deserved, which is the full truth... Obviously, I do not know what the full truth will be, but we will get it."

The MoD has previously said four studies found no increased health risks for those involved with the tests, as did a study carried out by Brunel University in 2022.

However, campaigners and veterans have accused the MoD of withholding full health records, including blood and urine tests, which they say would establish a link.

The MoD released some official documents in July 2026 , though it said some records may have been inadvertently destroyed three years earlier.

The department also said the medical records that veterans and their families were trying to access would appear "complex and inconsistent" as a central database was never held by the military, in part due to the intense Cold War-era security around the nuclear tests.

The independent panel announced on Tuesday will be be modelled on the Hillsborough Independent Panel and chaired by the same person, James Jones, the former Bishop of Liverpool.

He told BBC Newsnight: "The nuclear veterans have for decades made serious allegations against the state about what happened to them and to their descendants through the exposure to nuclear radiation. These merit serious investigation."

Downing Street said it would produce a report by October 2027 to coincide with the 75th anniversary of the first British nuclear weapons test.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: "It's taken too long to get here and I think today of the people who haven't lived to see this moment - and I fear for the people who might not see the outcome."

He acknowledged low trust in the MoD among veterans and their families, assuring them the department would not be involved with setting up the panel or defining its remit.

He said the panel would "help us to make sure that the cover-up is exposed".

Asked if the government would pay compensation should the panel recommend it, Streeting said he would not pre-judge its report but that he felt "absolutely sure the findings will be uncomfortable" and the government "will have to take that on the chin".

Radiation a 'hidden bullet' says testing veteran

articles.title: Worst airports for Thanksgiving travel chaos ranked as major US hubs top list
articles.summary: Chicago O'Hare topped a Thanksgiving travel study with a 96.73 Chaos Score, as delays hit nearly 28% of flights and averaged 93 minutes over three years.
articles.body: A new study has ranked the most disrupted U.S. airports for Thanksgiving travel — and Chicago O'Hare took the top spot, with several other major hubs rounding out the list. The rankings were recently compiled by digital travel service Nomad eSIM, as reported by local outlet Secret Chicago. HOLIDAY AIRFARE HITS 10-YEAR HIGH AS THANKSGIVING AND CHRISTMAS TRAVEL COSTS SOAR Coming in second place was John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York City, which had a 72.66 Chaos Score. Researchers found that almost 20% of JFK’s Google reviews were negative. Out of 53,462 reviews analyzed, there were 10,446 one- or two-star reviews. The study cited one Google review that ripped the airport for lack of customer service and inadequate terminal seating. articles.title: Ministers ask public for views on changing age of consent
articles.summary: Some campaigners have argued that different limits should apply, depending on the age gap between the people involved.
articles.body:
The government is inviting the public to share its views as ministers consider whether or not to stagger the age of consent.

Currently adults of any age are legally able to have sex with 16 and 17-year-olds, however some campaigners have argued that different limits should apply, depending on the age gap between the people involved.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he wanted survivors, parents, young people, victim support services and the wider public to "to share their experiences and inform this process".

The government is also announcing that new limits on non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) will come into force months earlier than originally planned.

The measures, which will now become law in January 2027, invalidate confidentiality clauses in new NDAs if they prevent employees from talking about harassment or discrimination or victims from reporting criminal conduct.

The changes will also cover NDAs signed outside of the workplace and mean that even if victims of crime have signed an NDA, it would not stop them from speaking to anyone, including the media, about what had happened.

Zelda Perkins, founder of the group Can't Buy My Silence, said the laws would "uphold the integrity of a legal system that must never be used to protect perpetrators at the expense of victims".

Perkins has previously said she felt forced to sign an NDA, which prevented her talking about abuse carried out by her former boss, the film producer Harvey Weinstein.

In 2017, she told the BBC she had tried to speak out about Weinstein's behaviour towards a co-worker but was told by lawyers she "didn't have a chance" due to signing an NDA.

The government has also said it is actively looking at whether to change the law on the age of consent and that it will ask members of the public for their opinions in the new year.

Burnham said: "I not only want to make sure victims can speak out about their own abuse, but also have the opportunity to challenge the status quo."

Earlier this month, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said there was "some common sense" about staggering the age of consent but questioned whether a new law could be enforced.

She also said it was "very confusing" to see Labour ministers talk about staggering the age of consent for sexual relations while at the same time lowering the voting age to 16.

Some countries around the world have a staggered age of consent. In Canada the age of consent for sexual activity is 16 years-old but a 14 or 15-year-old can consent to sexual activity as long as the partner is less than five years older.

Recent high-profile cases including Russell Brand's rape conviction and allegations made against David Walliams have prompted conversations about both the age of consent and NDAs.

Mia Latter, a woman who alleges she was raped by Brand when she was 16 and he was 30, has called for the age of consent to be changed.

Latter is one of six women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation.

Brand denied the allegations at the time and none of the six women were complainants in Brand's recent criminal trial.

In the same week that Brand was convicted, ITV News and the Guardian reported that David Walliams had been accused of sexual misconduct by several women.

One woman said she now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault". Walliams strongly denied he had any sexual contact with the girl.

Walliams said he rejected any allegations of criminal activity and that he has never engaged in the grooming of young women.

In late 2023, Walliams' publisher HarperCollins started an internal inquiry about the author's alleged inappropriate behaviour with young female staff.

A female staff member left the company with a pay-out and an NDA.

A spokesperson for the publisher has said: "HarperCollins UK previously terminated its publishing relationship with David Walliams.

"We take the safety of our people incredibly seriously and to respect the privacy of individuals we do not comment on employee matters."

articles.title: Sheikh Hasina plans December 16 return, Dhaka signals only extradition route
articles.summary: TOI Correspondent from Dhaka: Former Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina on Tuesday declared she plans to head home on December 16, when the country
articles.body: TOI Correspondent from Dhaka: Former Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina on Tuesday declared she plans to head home on December 16, when the country celebrates its independence from Pakistan, only to be met with yet another sign that the governing BNP is not quite keen on the Awami League boss's return, notwithstanding their declared intent to carry out the death sentence awarded to her.Following through on her earlier statement that she would be home by the year-end and was ready to face consequences, Hasina asked Dhaka to arrange her air travel from India on national carrier Biman Bangladesh, the former PM's spokesperson Syed Mozammel Ali said in a statement.Hasina's 'December 16' announcement - the first time she gave a date of return - triggered strong reactions in Dhaka, with state minister for foreign affairs Humaiun Kobir Tuesday saying that "she can only be brought back through extradition, in handcuffs" and stressing "reality and desire are two different things".‘No plane, copter, bus, car or rickshaw for Hasina’Everyone knows that Hasina is a terrorist and that terrorism is sponsored by her from New Delhi,” Kobir told a news conference at the foreign ministry.Not many were, however, impressed, considering that the extradition route is used to bring back those who may not be willing to return. “Have you ever heard of a situation where the accused herself is willing to return to face trial, yet the receiving country insists on extradition, especially when the extradition process is unlikely to succeed or, at the very least, could take a long time? Does that make any sense at all?”Awami League functionary and former cabinet minister Mohammad Ali Arafat asked.Shama Obaed Islam, also a state minister for foreign affairs, said that “govt has not made any arrangements with anyone to send a plane, helicopter, bus, car, or rickshaw. Is that clear?”. She, while addressing the presser, said all Bangladesh missions abroad are considered “Bangladesh territory”, and Hasina would face arrest if she appears at any of those missions.PM’s information and broadcasting adviser Zahed Ur Rahman said govt had no communication with Hasina over her return and was holding discussions with India on the issue. “Let me tell you clearly... if this particular individual, or any other convicted person, returns, they will be treated as accused; they will be arrested immediately and sent to jail — to the central jail. There will be no deviation from this,” Shama Obaed said, referring to a special tribunal sentencing Hasina to death in 2025. Kobir said the reality is that a terrorist will never be allowed to come back other than through extradition. “The desire may be there...coming on foot or by flight. No, she is not a regular commercial passenger. She can only be brought back in handcuffs,” he said.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: China-linked network using AI fakes to smear Taiwan election candidates, BBC Verify finds
articles.summary: The network attacked key figures in the ruling DPP, including President Lai and mayoral candidate Shen.
articles.body:
Taiwan's ruling party is being repeatedly targeted with AI videos spreading false claims about its leader and other key members ahead of crucial local elections, BBC Verify has found.

A China-linked network has pumped out more than 500 fake videos about the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) in the past year, which experts suggest is part of a long-running campaign to influence the outcome of the elections.

The videos appear to try to smear President Lai Ching-te by claiming he holds a US green card - and would abandon Taiwan if war broke out with China - which Taiwan's presidential office says is completely false. Deepfakes also appear to show Puma Shen, who is running to be the mayor of capital Taipei, using drugs, which he denies. Others seek to undermine or ridicule the politicians by showing them in children's clothing or as popular film characters.

The Taipei mayoralty has traditionally served as a springboard to the presidency. Experts say this has made Shen, who has been openly critical of Beijing, an obvious target for disinformation campaigns. The current mayor, Chiang Wan-an, is part of Taiwan's Kuomintang (KMT) party, which favours closer ties with China.

Taiwan is a self-governing island that China claims as part of its territory. Beijing and Taipei have long observed an uneasy status quo under which Taiwan, backed by the US, neither formally declares independence nor unites with China.

But tensions have risen since the DPP came to power in 2016. Beijing has repeatedly accused the party of pursuing independence while China's leader Xi Jinping, who has said "reunification" with Taiwan is a key goal, has stepped up pressure against the party with increased military activity around the island.

Experts believe the current disinformation activity is part of a broader campaign against Taiwan designed to undermine trust in its democratic process.

"The account operators are trying to make people distrust the DPP politicians so that they will not believe whatever they say," Austin Horng-En Wang, an expert in cognitive warfare at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, told BBC Verify. "If you don't trust that candidate then you will not listen to what they say," he added.

The videos, many of which were shared from an account called "noxparable" or carried a watermark with the same name, have been viewed tens of millions of times across several social media platforms since May 2025.

More than half of those views were tracked in the past four months as the activity has ramped up ahead of the elections. Many of the accounts involved in spreading disinformation listed their locations on social media as mainland China and Hong Kong, while a number of the clips carried labels showing they were generated with AI. Many people who engaged with the videos were often seen repeating the false claims or attacking DPP figures in the comments, while others appeared to treat the clips as entertainment.

One of the most widely shared videos targeted Shen by superimposing his face onto a man who is seen holding a lighter and exhaling smoke alongside claims he is smoking drugs. The video appears to build on accusations from Taiwan's opposition party that he supports drugs decriminalisation, which Shen denies, and was debunked by a local news network.

Shen has taken legal action against people sharing deepfakes, local media reported, while his campaign office said AI videos showing the candidate appeared to be part of a "classic tactic China uses to smear specific targets". BBC Verify contacted the Chinese embassy in London for comment.

Other debunked claims include allegations that Lai's predecessor Tsai Ing-wen had fraudulently obtained her PhD from the London School of Economics. The university pushed back on identical allegations in 2019 and confirmed it had awarded her the doctorate.

A number of the social media accounts BBC Verify identified as sharing the disinformation videos appeared to be linked to Chinese firm Borderless, which produces websites that blend apolitical content with pro-China messaging. The network has also been investigated by journalists at the Taiwanese independent media outlet The Reporter, who shared their findings with BBC Verify. Borderless has previously been accused of carrying out "cognitive warfare" against Taiwan by Taipei's National Security Bureau and the firm has been contacted for comment.

Analysts confirmed to BBC Verify there were also linguistic clues that the accounts, which presented themselves as based in Taiwan, were actually posting from China. The posts occasionally used a simplified Chinese script introduced by the Communist government which was never adopted in Taiwan.

The posts mostly appeared during regular office hours, which Wang suggested showed a "professional" operation, while the accounts originating outside Taiwan showed evidence of election interfering. "When they pretended to be citizens in another country and used these accounts to manipulate the public opinion of the other country during the campaign, it is definitely election interference," Wang added.

Earlier this month, Taiwan's central election commission aired an advert warning voters to "beware of AI-generated deepfake videos" circulating online that could seek to influence the upcoming election. It comes as government officials flagged nearly 2,700 social media accounts to Meta that it claimed were part of a Chinese information warfare campaign, Reuters reported. Meta said it had removed the accounts.

Andrew Yeh of the China Strategic Risk Institute said the ultimate goal is not to favour any party. "China's information operations succeed not just by backing one candidate or opposing another, but by diluting Taiwan's policy debates, driving polarisation and degrading Taiwanese citizens' trust in their democratic processes," he said.

"Regardless of whether the KMT or DPP comes out on top, a more fractured and more divided Taiwan is in Beijing's interests."

articles.title: South Africa convicts Zimbabwean who tried to fight Ukraine for Russia
articles.summary: The Zimbabwean man was arrested on November 8 at a Johannesburg airport while attempting to board a flight to Russia.
articles.body:
A South African court has convicted and sentenced a Zimbabwean man for trying to travel to Russia to fight in Ukraine after he was arrested earlier this month alongside eight others.

Tafadzwa Sithole was sentenced to five years in prison on Tuesday, under a five-year suspension, meaning he would only have to serve the time if he is convicted of a similar crime within that time period. Sithole is set to be deported back to Zimbabwe.

He told the court that he had agreed to fight for Russia in the war in exchange for “remuneration” after successfully applying online in Zimbabwe.

“He knew that the Russian Federation was engaged in an ongoing armed conflict with Ukraine and that the military service he intended to render would be performed in the context of that armed conflict,” his lawyer told the court.

Sithole was arrested at OR Tambo international airport on November 8 while attempting to board a flight to Russia.

Sithole said a person he identified as “Albina” contacted him after he submitted the application, arranged accommodation in South Africa and provided a flight ticket to Russia. His admissions were detailed in a plea agreement with South African prosecutors.

He pleaded guilty to violating the Regulation of Foreign Military Assistance Act. The act prohibits mercenary activity and regulates military assistance to parties in foreign conflicts, including recruitment and training, and also applies to foreign nationals.

Sithole, who described himself as an unemployed third-year student at a university in Zimbabwe, appeared in court with four other accused who are also negotiating plea agreements with prosecutors.

He said he entered South Africa legally on November 4 and stayed in an accommodation in Kempton Park, east of Johannesburg, in preparation for his travel to Russia.

Zimbabwe is among several African countries where Russia has been recruiting fighters for its war against Ukraine. Others include South Africa, Kenya, Botswana and Ghana.

Zimbabwean authorities said in March that 15 citizens had been killed in the war in Ukraine and that they were seeking the return of 66 others. The government said recruits were promised well-paid jobs but had their travel documents confiscated and were forced into combat.

Kenya ’s government said in February that more than 1,000 citizens had been recruited to fight for Russia. Families protested in Nairobi in March, demanding their relatives’ return and the prosecution of those responsible.

An investigation by Code for Africa, a nonprofit data journalism and technology organisation, identified 289 websites, domains and social media profiles used to lure recruits through false advertising and promises of generous benefits.

articles.title: Thomas Markle indicted in US for possessing child sex abuse images
articles.summary: The FBI arrested Markle on 6 November after a search of a storage unit he had allegedly rented in Los Angeles uncovered the abuse material.
articles.body:
Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex has been indicted by a federal grand jury in Los Angeles for possessing child sex abuse images.

Markle, who remains in custody in Florida, allegedly possessed materials that include at least one image involving a prepubescent minor and a minor under 12 years old, court documents filed in California show.

The 82-year-old has denied possessing images of child sex abuse. He is expected to be arraigned in Los Angeles in the coming weeks.

Last week, a judge in Florida declared Prince Harry's father-in-law mentally competent to stand trial.

The FBI arrested Markle on 6 November at an elderly care home in Florida on a single federal charge of possessing child sexual abuse material. He now faces two counts.

His arrest came after a search of a storage unit he had allegedly rented in Los Angeles for almost two decades uncovered the abuse material.

Markle was initially released on conditional bail but was then ordered to stay in jail pending trial after allegedly removing a location monitoring device.

In the indictment, filed by the US Attorney's Office in the Central District of California, Markle is accused of knowingly possessing 35mm film negatives on 30 October and 4 November that contained child sexual abuse materials.

The US Attorney's Office said that during both instances Markle allegedly knew the images contained such materials.

Inside the storage units, federal agents found two images that depict an adult man - whom a witness identified as Markle - with an underage child, the US attorney's office said.

They also alleged that a third image appears to depict a child in a room believed to be part of a motel chain in the Philippines. Markle moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and he lived in Cebu until May.

"The affidavit also describes additional photographs that appear to show Markle with children in various stages of undress," prosecutors said.

articles.title: One in three 16 to 24-year-olds in Britain have never had sex
articles.summary: More young people in Britain have never had sex, but many are sexting and watching porn.
articles.body:
British people, particularly teens and young adults, are having less or no sex compared to past generations, but lots are watching porn and sexting, a major study reveals.

It is the first time The National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles' ( Natsal ) research into general public sex lives has asked about online behaviours.

Half of people aged 16 to 24 have sent or received sexual images on their phone in the last year, while one in two young women and almost nine in 10 young men say they have viewed pornography.

But a third of this age group have never had sex, up from a fifth in the last study 12 years ago.

Adults under 45 are having less sex too, doing it twice a month, on average, down from once a week in 1990.

More than one in three (37%) women said they had watched porn in the past year.

For men, it was around four in every five (81%).

Among the 16-24 year-olds, half of women and most young men (86%) said they watched it.

Porn use and masturbation were less common among people who had never had sex, which the authors say suggests solo and online activity is not simply replacing in-person sex, although they cannot be sure.

They didn't ask about AI or virtual relationships with romantic chatbots, but say they probably should next time.

Soazig Clifton, one of the Natsal team and from University College London, said: "When we did our fieldwork in 2022-24 that seemed a little bit sci-fi.

"In the future we might be looking at the impact of AI on people's sexual behaviour and on their relationships, thinking about things like AI companions."

Co-researcher Prof Wendy Macdowall, from the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine (LSHTM), says while it may be tempting to blame screen time for less sex, it's likely many other factors are involved, "especially for young people."

Young people are drinking less alcohol than past generations and more live at home with their parents, for example.

Rising rates of mental health conditions might also be involved, along with the Covid pandemic that stopped people going out.

She says more open discussion of consent could also mean young people feel better able to decide whether and when to have sex.

But some are troubled by their sex lives.

One in seven women (14%) reported ongoing upset with others about things done to them in their sexual past.

The same proportion of men reported feeling shame about some of their sexual thoughts and desires.

This fourth Natsal survey reveals trends, but cannot fully explain them.

The previous one, in 2010, suggested having sex too soon was the biggest regret of young people losing their virginity.

Now, it appears more are waiting longer.

Almost two in five young women (38%) and more than one in four young men (28%) now report never having had sex. That is up from around one in five in the earlier surveys of 1990, 2000 and 2010.

And among all adults who are having sex, most are doing it less often. The average used to be once a week. Now, it's fortnightly.

The latest results, published in The Lancet and based on a survey of 6,700 people aged 16-59 selected at random across Britain, reveal:

three-quarters of adults have had sex in the past year

the average number of sexual partners in a lifetime is five

women have sex once a month and men twice a month, on average

reports of sex with a same-sex partner have increased among both men and women, but by how much is less clear

Unprotected sex, but fewer want children

Many Brits, young people in particular, are having unprotected sex that can lead to pregnancies and sexually transmitted infections (STIs), the figures suggest.

And use of the oral contraceptive pill has declined among young women.

But more women now say they do not want children - a doubling in the past decade, from 8% to 17% among those aged 16–44.

"Understanding what's driving this – whether economic insecurity, climate anxiety or changing life priorities – should now be a priority for future research and policy, as it has real implications for planning health, care and family services," says researcher Dr Laura Oakley from the LSHTM.

articles.title: Rebel group retreats in DR Congo after heavy clashes with government forces
articles.summary: CRP halts advance towards Bunia, citing commitments made during Ugandan-mediated talks with government.
articles.body:
The rebel group led by convicted war criminal Thomas Lubanga has withdrawn from areas recently seized in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) after days of heavy fighting with government forces.

The Convention for the Popular Revolution (CRP) announced on Tuesday that it had decided to halt an advance towards the town of Bunia, the capital of Ituri province in northeast DRC.

In a statement, the group cited a commitment made in talks with the Congolese government, mediated by Uganda’s President Yoweri Museveni, as one of the reasons for its withdrawal.

The CRP’s decision came one day after the group seized the Iga-Barriere, a strategic area about 25km north of Bunia, forcing government troops to withdraw towards the provincial capital.

Lubanga, a former leader of the Union of Congolese Patriots, was convicted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) in 2012 on charges of recruiting and using child soldiers.

He was sentenced to 14 years in prison and released in March 2020 after completing his sentence. Lubanga remains sanctioned by the United Nations.

Lubanga announced the formation of the CRP in 2025, opening another front against the DRC’s President Felix Tshisekedi.

The group said the decision to withdraw troops was made “out of respect for the commitments made at the State House” by the Congolese government and the CRP, referring to an October 9 meeting hosted by Uganda between Lubanga and a delegation of senior government and military officials.

On Sunday, the World ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌Health Organization said fighting near a hospital in the Ituri ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠province, north of Bunia, forced the evacuation of health workers and aid partners, disrupting Ebola response efforts.

The DRC is experiencing its largest and deadliest Ebola outbreak, which has spread across the country’s east and northeast. Ituri remains one of the most affected provinces.

Thousands of civilians have reportedly been displaced towards Bunia since the weekend due to renewed fighting between rebel fighters and government forces, according to local media reports.

articles.title: Bill Maher declares late-night comedy is 'dead' after major political shift
articles.summary: HBO host Bill Maher agreed with Piers Morgan that late-night comedy was "dead," saying partisan hosts like Jimmy Kimmel won't play to half the country.
articles.body: HBO host and comedian Bill Maher told Piers Morgan Tuesday that late-night comedy was "dead" due to comedians focusing too much on one-sided political jokes. Maher and Morgan discussed the state of late-night shows since Johnny Carson retired from "The Tonight Show" in 1992. Maher remarked that Carson likely retired at the right time before hosts and even entertainers became determined to force political messaging into their shows. "Do you think that the likes of Jimmy Kimmel and the others, by being so obviously politically partisan, have they conspired to slightly kill late-night comedy for you?" Morgan asked Maher on "One on One with Piers Morgan." JOHNNY CARSON'S FRIEND SAYS LATE-NIGHT KING WISELY AVOIDED PARTISANSHIP AS KIMMEL CONTROVERSY GROWS "Well, it definitely seems dead," Maher said. "Yeah, so I don't think that helped. I know they don't like it when I say that, but it's true." Maher remarked that he was always political on his programs but distanced himself from other late-night hosts since they had no interest in appealing to people outside their political circle. "Now I'm like, 'Oh, I'm glad I'm not lumped in' because I'm not like them at all. I'm really not. And I'm not saying they're not talented or funny. They are. But, yeah, they absolutely have no interest in playing to half the country," Maher said. Morgan pointed out that an overwhelming number of Kimmel's late-night political guests were not Republicans and that hosts like Kimmel rarely joke about Democrats. LENO SAYS HE GETS 'BEAT UP' RHETORICALLY FOR REFUSING TO GO POLITICAL BUT REFUSES TO ALIENATE TRUMP AUDIENCES "It's not like the left isn't doing a lot of stuff. And, of course, I've lost fans on the far left, and I don't miss them. You know what? Because if you don't understand what's wrong with your own side, you are watching the wrong show," Maher said. Fox News Digital reached out to ABC and Kimmel's representative for comment. Media Research Center President David Bozell agreed with Maher, citing his organization's history of documenting liberal bias on late-night shows. "For years, MRC has documented just how predictable late-night television has become. The same people are always the punchline, and the same people are almost never the punchline. Somewhere along the way, the networks confused applause from a few hundred people in a studio with entertainment for millions of Americans at home," Bozell said. BILL MAHER TELLS LIBERALS TO STOP 'PARTISAN SULKING' AND JOIN AMERICA 250 PARTY Earlier this year, Maher suggested his friendship with Kimmel was on the rocks after he criticized Kimmel's wife, Molly McNearney, for cutting off family relationships based on whether they voted for President Donald Trump. articles.title: Fort Hood mass shooter makes legal move to stop Pentagon’s firing squad execution
articles.summary: The former Army officer whose scheduled military execution by firing squad provoked outrage over an initial proposal to livestream his death is planning to file a constitutional challenge that could halt his December execution, his lawyers said Tuesday.
articles.body: The former Army officer whose scheduled military execution by firing squad provoked outrage over an initial proposal to livestream his death is planning to file a constitutional challenge that could halt his December execution, his lawyers said Tuesday. Nidal Hasan, convicted in the 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, that claimed 13 lives, filed a motion for a stay of execution so he can submit what’s known as a habeas corpus petition, which requires the government to justify a person’s detainment. “There is no question that the violence committed at Fort Hood caused unimaginable pain and loss,” Anna Arceneaux, deputy director of the ACLU’s Capital Punishment Project, said in a statement. “But the gravity of that loss does not change the government’s obligation to uphold the principles that define our justice system. Mr. Hasan, like every person facing an irreversible punishment, must have a chance to pursue federal review of his case.” Hasan, 56, had officially exhausted his military justice appeals, opening the door to President Donald Trump in October approving his death sentence and the Army setting an execution date. Hasan’s request was filed in civilian court, which is another process available to military prisoners. Military experts told NBC News the legal maneuver to file a habeas corpus petition would all but assure Hasan’s case will be tied up in a lengthy review process that could effectively stall his pending execution to well beyond the end of Trump’s term. At that point, they say, Trump’s successor may avoid setting another execution date. The motion was filed on behalf of Hasan by the ACLU of Kansas. Pentagon and Army officials could not immediately be reached for comment. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth first raised the prospect of livestreaming Hasan’s execution, telling a conservative news outlet that he would ensure “people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.” But John Baker, the federal public defender for the Western District of North Carolina whose capital habeas unit is assisting Hasan, said the case deserves further review by a federal court. “The President, the Secretary of Defense, and others have turned Mr. Hasan’s case into a political spectacle,” Baker said in a statement. “Our government cannot be permitted to execute Mr. Hasan until his death sentence has received full and fair review, which the Constitution safeguards through our federal courts.” Few details were made available about how a firing squad execution could unfold, although Army officials said it would occur at 1 p.m. Dec. 3 at Fort Hood — around the time the attack occurred at the military base. During the shooting, Hasan was injured by responding officers and paralyzed and now requires a wheelchair. Within days of Hegseth’s announcement, Trump said he would ultimately decide whether Hasan’s death could potentially be watched by millions of people online. He subsequently said in a Truth Social post that while livestreaming the execution “might have been a strong deterrent,” there are other people who “would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device.” “He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad,” the president said, “but this event will not be streamed.” Hegseth’s announcement had set off immediate backlash from a bipartisan group of lawmakers, human rights organizations and religious leaders, many of whom said a livestreamed execution would be “medieval” and “barbaric,” echoing public killings conducted by the most brutal totalitarian regimes and terror states and harkening back to the nation’s dark period of public lynchings and racism. In the U.S., the last large-scale gathering for a lawfully public execution occurred in 1936 in Kentucky, where a Black man convicted of raping a white woman was hanged in front of thousands, according to news reports. Opponents of livestreaming Hasan’s execution also warned it could be used as propaganda by jihadist militants, while playing into the desires of Hasan, an American-born Muslim who had become radicalized. “I’m paraplegic and could be in jail for the rest of my life,” Hasan told a mental health panel following the shooting spree. “However, if I died by lethal injection, I would still be a martyr.” The U.S. military has not put a service member to death by firing squad since 1945 and last executed a service member in 1961, by hanging. Both were conducted privately. Currently, four people, including Hasan, are on the military’s death row at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas.

articles.title: A charity vending-machine programme that began in 2017 has raised around $70 million worldwide; partners say donations of livestock and business training helped some families increase their incomes sevenfold
articles.summary: A vending machine in the US is dispensing something rather unusual this Christmas. No, it isn't a new flavour of chips or a limited-edition chocolate bar.
articles.body: A vending machine in the US is dispensing something rather unusual this Christmas. No, it isn't a new flavour of chips or a limited-edition chocolate bar. Instead, it is dispensing goats, chickens, school supplies, menstrual hygiene kits and even the beginnings of small businesses (how do they even fit all of that in such a tiny machine?).The happiness, however, is not necessarily enjoyed by the person standing in front of the machine. It travels thousands of miles away, sometimes to a family that has never even heard of the person who made the purchase.The Giving Machines, a charitable vending-machine initiative in the US, have been doing so since 2017. And nearly a decade later, the initiative has raised approximately $70 million for charities around the world, according to their press release.A vending machine that works in reverseThe Giving Machines were first introduced in November 2017 by The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints as part of its annual Light the World Christmas campaign. According to a 2017 report by Deseret News, the first machines were installed in the lobby of the Joseph Smith Memorial Building in Salt Lake City, Utah. Instead of the usual assortment of crisps and fizzy drinks, visitors could purchase things such as goats, chickens, food, clean water, medicines and eye examinations for people in need.At the time, a goat could be donated for $75, while two chickens cost $25. The charities partnered with the initiative would then arrange for the selected goods and services to reach their intended recipients.The idea was to make charitable giving as straightforward as buying something from a regular vending machine. As Brent H. Nielson, then executive director of the Church's Missionary Department, told Deseret News in 2017, people were accustomed to visiting vending machines to get something for themselves. This one offered them the opportunity to give something instead.It seems to have caught on. According to the Church's 2026 announcement, the Giving Machines are now entering their tenth season, with installations across 145 locations in 28 countries and six continents. More than 500 nonprofit organisations are participating, offering nearly 4,500 different items and services. The initiative has raised approximately $70 million since its beginning.From a couple of chickens to a family businessOf all the things one can purchase through these machines, livestock might be among the most interesting. A couple of chickens or a young goat might not sound like an especially extravagant gift, but for a family with limited opportunities to earn an income, they can be the beginning of something much bigger.Speaking to Deseret News in its November 22, 2026 report, Liz Mumford, a board member at Mentors International, explained how donations of goats, chickens and other livestock, combined with business mentoring, have helped families become financially independent. The organisation, which has worked in poverty alleviation for almost 35 years, has been part of the Giving Machine initiative for the past five.According to Mentors International's data, families receiving these products through the programme have experienced a sevenfold increase in their personal incomes. Along with the livestock, recipients also receive business training and mentoring to help them turn their resources into sustainable livelihoods.The organisation's 2026 Giving Machine programme includes everything from two chickens and baby goats to sewing, cooking and farming business kits. Each gift is paired with guidance from a local mentor, helping recipients understand how to use their new resources to earn money.To give someone a new resource to earn money and help them out through difficult times is one of the most heartwarming gestures. And, visiting the very people you helped, seeing something you had selected on a vending machine thousands of miles away become a real source of food and income for another family makes it all the more meaningful. A small act of generosity can go a long way.The gifts go well beyond food and farmingThe initiative is also helping women and girls access opportunities that are often taken for granted. Days for Girls International, a nonprofit working to improve menstrual health and education, has been participating in the programme for two years.Its CEO, Tiffany Larson, told Deseret News that donations of washable menstrual kits, postpartum kits and menstrual health education sessions had helped the organisation reach 28,000 additional girls in its first year of participation. In the following year, that number increased to 48,000.Their work is not just about providing menstrual products. It is about human dignity and unlocking the potential of women who might otherwise face barriers to education and everyday life.There is also a particularly personal motivation behind the work of the African Girls Hope Foundation, whose goal is to ensure that every African refugee and orphan girl who receives an AGHF scholarship is able to graduate from high school. Its founder, Grace Nkundabantu, told Deseret News that she understood what it meant to struggle for an education. She recalled being unable to afford school and being thrown out of her classroom every semester because of it.Today, her organisation provides scholarships, uniforms, educational materials, mentorship and counselling to girls across sub-Saharan Africa. Nkundabantu said that participating in the Giving Machine initiative over the past four years had increased the foundation's capacity to help more girls each year. For someone who once struggled to remain in a classroom herself, being able to help other girls stay in theirs seems like a full circle moment.Food assistance is another important part of the initiative. Claudio Silva, chief financial and operations officer at World Food Program USA, told Deseret News that the organisation received more than $400,000 in Giving Machine donations in 2024. The programme matched that amount with another $400,000, helping reach approximately 38,000 people.A little generosity goes a long wayThe Giving Machines are a reminder that giving back does not always have to involve a grand gesture. Sometimes, it is a few dollars, a couple of chickens or a school kit purchased by someone who simply wanted to help.As Thanksgiving approaches, the initiative is a timely reminder to appreciate the things we might otherwise overlook. Having enough food, being able to attend school and having the means to support a family are not universal comforts. And while we cannot solve every problem in the world, we can make somebody's circumstances a little easier.There is also some reassurance in knowing where the money goes. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints covers the operational costs of the machines, meaning 100% of the donations collected go to participating charities. The organisations are responsible for delivering the selected items and services and providing reports on how the money has been used.Those interested in seeing more of the initiative can follow its official Instagram account or visit the Giving Machines website, which shares stories of donations reaching families around the world.As Mother Teresa says, “Not all of us can do great things, but we can do small things with great love”. You might walk away from this vending machine without a single thing in your hands, but somewhere else, a family could be harvesting its first fruit, a girl could be returning to school or a woman could be starting a business of her own. And if a vending machine can make that happen, perhaps we could all do with a little less shopping for ourselves and a little more giving to others.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient.
